strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful and underexplored task: generating automotive radar point clouds with RCS and Doppler from multi-view camera imagery, which is relevant for scalable multimodal simulation and data augmentation.

The method is technically sensible and well motivated: it adapts an efficient latent diffusion backbone (SANA) to BEV radar maps, uses known Gaussian blurring with an IRL1/FISTA deconvolution step for sparse point recovery, and conditions on BEV-aligned depth, semantics, and motion cues from pretrained foundation models.
The proposed evaluation framework covers geometric fidelity, radar attribute fidelity, and distribution similarity, and includes useful ablations on kernel bandwidth and point-cloud recovery methods.

The generated radar data can be consumed by a detector trained on real radar, yielding non-trivial NDS (0.30) compared to a near-zero baseline, and the qualitative scene-editing examples show occlusion-aware changes in the radar response.
The paper is generally well structured and clear, with informative figures and an explicit limitations section that acknowledges dependence on upstream foundation models and hallucination risks.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely system-level: the work combines existing components (SANA, pretrained depth/segmentation/flow models, BEV projection, LASSO-style deconvolution) rather than introducing a substantially new algorithm or theoretical insight.

Experimental evidence is limited to a single dataset (MAN TruckScenes), with only 49 evaluation clips and 40 annotated frames, one radar configuration, and filtered-out night scenes, so generalizability across sensors, datasets, and conditions is not established.

The baseline is weak and potentially unfair: RGB2Point is a deterministic single-image point-cloud model adapted post hoc, trained for much less time, and not representative of recent radar-specific generation methods; stronger or more directly comparable baselines are missing.

Ablation results are mostly small and within noise: removing appearance, semantic, or velocity conditioning changes metrics only marginally, so the necessity and contribution of each conditioning cue are not convincingly demonstrated.

The downstream detection gap remains substantial: NDS 0.30 versus 0.48 on real radar, mAP 0.11 versus 0.38, and much worse velocity error (mAVE 4.04 versus 1.88); the practical benefit for perception is therefore still limited.
Scene editing is evaluated only qualitatively, with no quantitative test, user study, or downstream augmentation experiment showing that the edited radar data improves training or perception.

The method discards elevation and produces 2D BEV point clouds (x, y, RCS, Doppler), which limits claims about full 3D radar point-cloud generation; the handling of elevation or z-coordinates in the downstream detector is not fully specified.
The newly proposed metrics are ad hoc and not validated against standard radar evaluation protocols or human judgment, and several results have high variance relative to the reported gains.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code release is mentioned, and some important design choices, such as DA thresholds, sigma, and diffusion conditioning details, may be sensitive but are not fully analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: controllable generation of automotive radar point clouds from multi-view cameras for simulation and data augmentation.

The proposed pipeline is reasonably clear: BEV radar maps for density/RCS/Doppler, latent diffusion with an efficient SANA backbone, foundation-model-derived BEV conditioning, and deconvolution-based point cloud recovery.
The paper includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, runtime information, and discusses limitations such as dependence on upstream foundation models and hallucination in unseen regions.
Qualitative results and scene-editing examples suggest the method can produce semantically aligned radar responses and can sometimes support downstream detection on generated data.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence does not convincingly support the main claims. Quantitative improvements are often small or mixed: CD Full in Entire Area is worse than the baseline, DA F1 remains low (0.24), variance is large, and no significance tests are provided.

Downstream utility is not demonstrated at a convincing level. The detector trained on real radar drops from NDS 0.48 on real data to 0.30 on RadarGen samples, and supplementary detection results show mAP 0.11 vs 0.38 and mAVE 4.04 vs 1.88, indicating poor motion/Doppler realism.

Baseline and comparison setup are weak. The main comparison is an adapted object-centric RGB2Point model and an in-house multi-view condition variant; there is no comparison to existing radar point cloud generation methods, physics-based/data-driven radar simulators, or strong deterministic baselines. The near-zero baseline NDS also raises concerns about baseline training or evaluation.

The ablation study undermines the claimed importance of the proposed BEV conditioning. Removing appearance, semantic, or velocity maps changes many metrics only marginally, and the direct multi-view model can even outperform RadarGen on some attribute MMD metrics, calling into question the benefit of the complex conditioning pipeline.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (MAN TruckScenes), with only 40 annotated evaluation frames, and no cross-dataset or cross-sensor generalization is shown. The proposed metrics are self-defined and not benchmarked against standard radar generation evaluations.

The radar representation and recovery method rely on strong simplifications: RCS/Doppler are assigned via Voronoi tessellation, the density map is modeled as a Gaussian-blurred point set, and recovery assumes the diffusion output satisfies the same forward model. This may not reflect true radar scattering or stochasticity and requires more validation.

The paper overclaims relative to the evidence. Phrases such as 'first probabilistic diffusion framework' and 'realistic automotive radar point clouds' are not sufficiently supported, especially given the detection gap, qualitative-only scene-editing validation, and lack of physical/electromagnetic grounding.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. Hyperparameters are given, but code/models are not mentioned, and the evaluation uses a non-standard metric suite that would make independent comparison difficult.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and underexplored problem: probabilistic generation of automotive radar point clouds from multi-view camera images, including RCS and Doppler attributes.
The proposed BEV representation is well-motivated for sparse, non-grid radar data and enables reuse of an efficient image-latent diffusion backbone without modifying the pretrained autoencoder.

The conditioning design using foundation-model depth, semantics, and optical-flow-derived radial velocity is reasonable and is supported by ablations showing the contribution of the BEV scene representation.
The deconvolution-based point cloud recovery is a principled way to recover sparse points from the generated density map, and the ablation over sigma and recovery methods is informative.
The paper introduces a broad set of evaluation metrics covering geometry, radar attributes, and distribution similarity, and reports ablations, downstream detection, and scene-editing demonstrations.
The limitations section is honest about reliance on upstream foundation models, low-light failures, and possible hallucinations in unseen regions.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset, MAN TruckScenes, which may not represent the broader automotive radar domain; cross-dataset generalization or multiple radar configurations are not demonstrated.

The downstream detection results show a substantial gap between generated and real radar data (NDS 0.30 vs. 0.48), suggesting that generated point clouds are not yet fully compatible with perception models trained on real data.

The baseline comparison is relatively narrow, using only an adapted RGB2Point model; comparisons to physics-based radar simulators or other data-driven radar point cloud generation approaches are missing or only discussed qualitatively.

Several metrics are newly proposed and non-standard, making it difficult to assess absolute quality and compare against future work; some metric choices, such as MMD on selected attributes, require more justification.
The ablation table contains some counterintuitive results, e.g., removing certain conditions can improve some MMD values, which is not fully explained.
The scene-editing experiments are qualitative only and lack a quantitative protocol for measuring whether edits produce physically and semantically correct radar changes.
The method is not evaluated on video input or temporal consistency beyond two frames, although automotive radar applications are inherently sequence-based.
Inference cost is dominated by BEV conditioning map creation (~9 s per timestep), which may limit large-scale simulation or deployment despite the efficient diffusion backbone.
